codes.evidence_quote: A big part of the syllabus is made up of notated dance steps... There are sections on jaleo, palmas, castanets... and a large and quite complete list of definitions of flamenco and dance terms.
codes.target: the revised Theater Spanish and Flamenco Dance Syllabus
codes.rationale: The syllabus is framed as a structured learning resource that gives students and aficionados mediated access to flamenco dance knowledge, notation, terminology, and technique.

codes.evidence_quote: The revised edition is much larger, more complete, and makes a place for itself as a valuable reference work... I have only one critical suggestion to make... There are many typos and minor errors
codes.rationale: The passage explicitly evaluates the syllabus positively as a reference work while also criticizing its proofreading errors.

derived_analysis.target: the revised Theater Spanish and Flamenco Dance Syllabus

codes.evidence_quote: For being a true "flamenco" means being first an Andaluz or Andaluza at heart.
codes.rationale: The passage explicitly defines what counts as true flamenco and links that genuineness to Andalusian belonging.

codes.evidence_quote: in Andalucía, flamenco is everywhere. It is a way of life so deeply interwoven in the very fabric of Andalucian life, that it cannot be separated from it.
codes.rationale: The text frames flamenco through Andalusian collective identity and treats that identity as central to belonging and representation.

codes.evidence_quote: The visitor who tries to pry away "just" the music, or the dance, may fool himself into thinking he/she learned "flamenco", but will miss out on the essence of things.
codes.target: visitors who reduce flamenco to music or dance alone
codes.rationale: The passage draws an epistemic boundary between superficial outside learning and insider understanding of flamenco's essence.

possible_but_not_emitted.reason: Images of earth, mother's milk, and possible disappearance suggest rootedness and continuity, but the stronger visible function is defining authenticity and belonging rather than preserving a past tradition.

derived_analysis.target: flamenco as an Andalusian way of life

annotation_notes: The article uses a broad cultural definition of flamenco rather than reviewing a performance.

codes.target: Manuel Agujetas de Jerez and his video performance
codes.rationale: The passage canonizes Agujetas through legendary status, world fame, maestro language, dynastic placement, and historic value.

codes.evidence_quote: An educational "must" for guitarists and singers.

codes.evidence_quote: she grew up surrounded by great flamenco artists and learned the art of dance and life without losing rhythm, that is, with verve and authenticity.
codes.rationale: The passage attributes authenticity to Vargas's way of learning and embodying flamenco, not merely to a generic personal quality.

codes.evidence_quote: Are you a bailarina or a bailora? "I am a bailaora." What is the difference? "A bailaora dances always to guitar palmas pitos and with the voice of the cante."
codes.rationale: The interview uses the identity/category of bailaora to define a culturally specific performer role and its proper flamenco markers.

codes.evidence_quote: I have a spirit that makes me do flamenco from deep within... It's as though it takes over my body
codes.rationale: The passage defines flamenco quality through depth, bodily possession, suffering, and expressive transmission as aesthetic criteria.

possible_but_not_emitted.reason: The article notes that Vargas learned while surrounded by artists, but the visible passage does not clearly describe embodied/oral lineage transmission as an authorizing process.
There are distinctions between audience, stage, gypsy, paya, bailarina, and bailaora, but the clearest social function is identity framing rather than an insider/outsider boundary.

derived_analysis.target: Manuela Vargas and the bailaora role

annotation_notes: Ethnic identity discussion was coded only where it organizes flamenco role, representation, or expressive authority.

codes.evidence_quote: There's no one better qualified to give us a rundown on flamenco than Teodoro Morca... internationally-known flamenco dancer, choreographer and teacher.
codes.target: Teodoro Morca as an explainer of flamenco
codes.rationale: Morca is explicitly positioned as an authoritative teacher and expert able to explain flamenco to readers.

codes.evidence_quote: Basically, flamenco is the art, the song, the way of life of the people of Southern Spain
codes.rationale: The passage defines flamenco as a genuine way of life rooted in the people of Southern Spain rather than merely a dance form.

codes.evidence_quote: It's definitely an art form of an oppressed people, that's why it has a built-in drama and emotion.
codes.target: flamenco as the art of an oppressed people
codes.rationale: The text frames flamenco through a collective identity group and uses that identity to explain its emotional and cultural authority.

codes.evidence_quote: If you see good flamenco, you see someone becoming themselves in dance, music, song. It's a real immediate thing... It's the immediacy of feeling that really attracts people
codes.rationale: Morca names immediacy, feeling, drama, and self-revelation as criteria for recognizing good flamenco.

possible_but_not_emitted.reason: The article compares flamenco to other forms of exercise and ballet, but that comparison concerns bodily fitness rather than canon or hierarchy within flamenco.
